content: 1. A study involving 114 participants evaluated the impact of six 90-minute group wheelchair skills training programs (WSTP) conducted three weeks apart. The sessions were led by rehabilitation therapists, counselors, or peer counselors in the USA. The findings indicated that individuals with lower baseline skill levels and higher attendance rates demonstrated greater improvements in achieving individually set goals, as measured by the Goal Attainment Score (GAS). 2. Worobey et al. (2018) conducted a study in the USA with 87 manual and power wheelchair users who could independently transfer. Participants were divided into three groups: a web-based transfer training module group (44 participants), an individualized in-person transfer training group (59 participants), and a waitlist control group (11 participants). Both web-based and in-person training significantly improved transfer techniques compared to the control group. 3. Worobey et al. (2021) studied 188 wheelchair users (91 manual wheelchair users and 97 power wheelchair users) in the USA. Participants underwent two 90-minute group wheelchair maintenance training sessions. The training improved participants' capacity to perform maintenance tasks and their frequency of completing these tasks. Improvements were sustained at one, six, and twelve months post-training. 4. Beaudoin et al. conducted a pre-post study on wheelchair users, focusing on mobility, posture, and function. Peer-led, community-based manual wheelchair training improved wheelchair skills, self-efficacy, and satisfaction with participation but did not significantly impact quality of life. 5. Charlton et al. implemented a three-week manual wheelchair training program facilitated by occupational therapists or allied health assistants. The program improved wheelchair performance, confidence, and frequency of use, enhancing safety, independence, and quality of life for individuals with lower limb amputations. 6. Choi et al. conducted a study comparing preand post-training outcomes in wheelchair skills capacity and confidence. All participants showed significant improvements in these areas after the intervention. 7. Eshraghi, Sawatzky, and Mortenson (2021) in Canada evaluated a peer-led manual wheelchair maintenance training program involving 20 participants (5 mentors and 15 mentees). While no significant improvement was observed in the 3-cone test, participants reported increased confidence in performing wheelchair maintenance and teaching others. 8. MacGillivray et al. assessed a powered wheelchair mobility training program. Participants set 5-10 mobility-related goals and showed significant improvements in goal satisfaction immediately after training and maintained these improvements three months later. 9. Morgan et al. (2017) in the USA studied six manual wheelchair users with spinal cord injuries. They underwent nine 90-minute training sessions focusing on wheelchair propulsion biomechanics. No significant differences in wheelchair skills were observed post-training. 10. Rice et al. (2020) in the USA evaluated a 12-week intervention for 18 manual wheelchair users with spinal cord injuries. The program focused on transfer skills and seated postural control. All outcomes, including mobility, posture, and quality of life, improved significantly after the intervention. 11. Sarigul-Klijn et al. (2017) in the USA trained individuals with chronic stroke and severe arm impairments to drive a bimanual wheelchair. Over six training sessions, participants significantly increased their speed and competence without experiencing pain. 12. Sawatzky et al. (2012) in Canada studied six children with spinal cord problems. A nine-hour wheelchair skills training program over two days significantly improved wheelchair skills and reduced pain and fatigue, as measured by the Impact Questionnaire. 13. Sawatzky, Mortenson, and Wong (2018) in Canada evaluated a 30-minute training session for 11 manual wheelchair users on using a rear-mounted power assist. While no significant differences were observed in confidence or skills, participants rated the training experience positively. 14. Hasdai, Jessel, and Weiss (1998) in Israel studied 22 children with disabilities (progressive muscular dystrophy or cerebral palsy). A computer simulator training program significantly improved driving performance in children without prior powered wheelchair experience. 15. Chang et al. (2020) in China analyzed retrospective data from 130 individuals with spinal cord injuries who underwent two rehabilitation periods. Significant improvements in basic life skills and their application in family and social life were observed during the second rehabilitation period. 16. Taylor et al. (2015) in the USA evaluated wheelchair satisfaction among children. Most participants reported satisfaction with the fit and function of their wheelchairs after 12 months of follow-up. 17. Webster et al. (2001) in the USA studied 40 patients with unilateral neglect. A computer-assisted training program focusing on wheelchair skills and obstacle avoidance improved participants' performance on a real-life wheelchair obstacle course compared to a control group. 18. Bazant et al. conducted a cross-sectional study in the Philippines based on WHO 2008 guidelines. Training improved activities of daily living and reduced secondary complications, such as falls, among wheelchair users.
